title: On the Growing Claims of Lockheed's Secret Fleet of Space Alien Flying Saucers
excerpt: ​In the wake of Jay Stratton’s new memoir Out of the Shadows , which debuted at number 2 on the New York Times bestseller list (BookScan sales totals won’t be available until next week),...
content:
​In the wake of Jay Stratton’s new memoir Out of the Shadows, which debuted at number 2 on the New York Times bestseller list (BookScan sales totals won’t be available until next week), Stratton has been on a media tour claiming that defense contractor Lockheed Martin has twelve flying saucers in storage and a secret program to reverse engineer them. Stratton claimed that former Lockheed executive Jim Ryder, who died almost a decade ago, had approached him in the 2000s, revealed the existence of the program, and proposed transferring a flying saucer to Stratton’s AAWSAP team for research, a proposal that the CIA blocked. 

​Over the past couple of days UFO advocate and researcher Marik von Rennenkampff took me to task on X for doubting this claim. Von Rennenkampff claimed that the assertion had been confirmed by a wide range of UFO figures who all told the same story and therefore is almost certainly true. However, the claim, which emerged in 2023, has gradually grown over time, and the earliest versions are not fully compatible with Stratton’s version.

 First, it’s important to note that Ryder is dead and cannot speak for himself. He left no public record of any of the claims, despite having spoken widely about many bizarre pseudoscience topics prior to his 2018 death. Similarly, the CIA official alleged to have scuttled the UFO transfer, Glenn Gaffney, denied any involvement. Of course, conspirators would claim that this is merely part of the conspiracy, and Gaffney is lying. Another pillar of the story, that Ryder’s boss was Ben Rich, who believed in ET flying saucers and that America had reverse-engineered them, is also questionable. There is no record that Ryder ever reported to Rich, who once headed Lockheed’s Skunkworks, and quotations attributed to Rich about ETs, UFOs, and reverse-engineering are known only from secondhand sources and are of dubious provenance.

 The conspiracy theory about Lockheed Martin (and its predecessor company, Lockheed) holding UFO wreckage originated only a few years ago, though it builds on older claims. It’s deep origins trace back to Silas Netwon’s infamous postwar hoax claiming the government had recovered intact flying saucers. At the same time, Lockheed’s famous Skunk Works was responsible for developing U.S. fighter jets like the SR-71, which was tested at Area 51 in Nevada, giving rise to UFO stories. But the specific claim that Lockheed held crashed saucer wreckage does not appear in the literature before 2020.

 The first rumbling occurred when the Wikileaks dump of John Podesta’s emails revealed that senior Lockheed Martin executive Rob Weiss, then the head of Skunkworks, was in contact with Blink-182’s Tom Delonge about UFOs. (Delonge initiated contact, and Weiss reportedly kept him at a polite distance.) Then in 2019, with the publication of the so-called Wilson-Davis memo, itself dubious, in which Adm. Thomas Wilson, the former head of the DIA, allegedly told AAWSAP’s Eric Davis just after he left office in 2002 that an unnamed contractor held “alien hardware.” Wilson, after stating that he could not name the “top” aerospace contractor he was discussing, supposedly said: “I told [them] I read their program record in the OUSDAT special program records group and wanted to know about their crashed UFO program, what their role in that was, what they had, etc. Also asked if they heard of MJ-12 or some such organization code related to crashed/recovered UFO craft.”

 This is the origin point for the allegation. However, this claim was allegedly made in the context of Philip J. Corso’s equally dubious claim in 1997’s The Day After Roswell that Hughes, Bell Labs, and IBM had received technologies derived from Roswell wreckage, and Wilson, of course, denied having said any of this, which ufologists took to be further confirmation of the conspiracy.

 As you can see, there was no specific claim about Lockheed holding intact flying saucers circulating prior to 2020, though the building blocks were there. The specific claim emerged in April 2020 when an unnamed BAASS employee who also worked for AAWSAP told Debrief cofounder Tim McMillan that the Atomic Energy Commission transferred crashed UFO material to Lockheed in 1977 to avoid having the craft exposed when Jimmy Carter made the AEC into a government department (the Department of Energy) in 1979. McMillan noted at the time that there was no evidence for the claim.

 However, the next year Eric Davis—who later reversed himself—claimed that McMillan’s BAASS source was misinformed, telling Joe Murgia in 2021: “McMillan’s BAASS source (an alleged former BAASS employee) is quite ill-informed and not in the know about the history of the legacy UAP recovery and reverse engineering studies program, because this particular topic is way above the pay grade and need-to-know access of the alleged former BAASS employee. This alleged former BAASS employee either fabricated his/her claims about Lockheed Aircraft Co., the AEC/DoE, and Jimmy Carter from out of whole cloth or he/she is reporting someone else’s uninformed opinions or he/she is reporting very old, unfounded rumors that circulate widely within UFOlogy.”

 In April 2021, former Sen. Harry Reid, who had used his office to create and fund AAWSAP, told The New Yorker that he had heard claims about Lockheed hiding a UFO for “decades” and that he had intervened to request an upgrade in AAWSAP’s security status so they could “take a look” at “retrieved materials” Lockheed might have, a request the DIA denied, finding there was no justification for the request. When that interview created controversy, Reid gave another a few days later in which he denied that Lockheed had any UFO materials and stated that he did not believe the claims that he sought to help AAWSAP investigate. His second statement was in line with prior comments, including a 2019 radio interview answering a question from Joe Murgia, in which he denied the U.S. had any crashed UFOs.

 At this point, the claim was now publicly circulating, but exactly what Lockheed supposedly held wasn’t quite clear to the group of ufologists circulating the claim. In 2023, James Lacatski, who ran AAWSAP and worked for the DIA, wrote in a document later entered in to the Congressional Record that the items to be transferred were “crash retrieval material,” not a complete UFO. (The document in question does not identify who wrote it, but in 2024, Lue Elizondo entered into the Congressional Record information that the paragraph was Lacatski’s.)

The $22M allocated for DIA AAWSAP, after speaking to multiple individuals on the program, was originally intended to SCIF-out Bigelow Aerospace Facilities in Las Vegas due to a UAP material divestment plan proposed to AAWSAP leadership by Lockheed Martin Space Systems Vice President Dr. James Ryder (now deceased). A specific facility known to me was described as having crash retrieval material from the 1950s and other historical operations. They proposed a technology transfer agreement (TTA) into the proposed Waived PSAP Sen Reid was championing (See DIA FOIA release).

 Unfortunately, due to the sensitive nature of the TTA, USDI and OSD leadership were not specifically briefed on this proposal. This is why, in “Skinwalkers at the Pentagon”, they approach DHS S&T, Tara O’Toole to set up a PSAP. Ultimately the original government custodian, CIA DS&T, disapproved that transfer during a meeting with Glenn Gaffney while he was in that position. Instead, much of the money was used to produce Defense Intelligence Reference Documents (DIRDs) to possibly show value to the Legacy Program.

​However, also in 2023, in a Weaponized podcast interview, Lacatski claimed that the U.S. had a captured flying saucer and that someone had entered it. Eric Davis asserted that Lacatski had personally entered the craft, which Lacatski decline to confirm. In his book that year, Skinwalkers at the Pentagon, Lacatski did not make reference to Lockheed as holding such a craft or Gaffney as preventing its transfer.

 David Grusch, in 2024, told Joe Rogan that the materials to be transferred were “bits and pieces,” perhaps including debris from a “hull,” and that he had seen documentation to that effect. It was decidedly not a complete and intact craft.

 Later in 2024, Lue Elizondo testified to Congress that he had heard the story after the fact but did not have any additional information beyond what the same people told him: “What I can say is that it was blocked. Why it was blocked, I can only surmise. I was part of some conversations later on with some of those contract personnel where they had told all of us that is accurate.” In a written follow-up sent to Congress, Elizondo amended his claim and add Lacatski’s 2023 statement, implying Lacatski was Elizondo’s source. At the same hearing, Michael Gold a lawyer who formerly was a deputy administrator at NASA, testified that he had never spoken to Ryder and did not have any conversations about UFOs.

 In 2025, George Knapp repeated the main story but added the Robert Bigelow himself negotiated the transfer, a claim no previous claimant had made. He gave the following testimony to Congress: “So, looking into the idea of crash retrievals and reverse engineering, while AAWSAP, that program, was active, the DIA’s contractor, Robert Bigelow of Las Vegas, made a bold attempt to acquire physical proof of UFO crashes. It has been widely reported and suspected that Lockheed Martin is one of the contractors—the defense contractors, that has held this stuff, stored it away in secrecy, and tried to figure out how it works. I have confirmed on the record that Robert Bigelow and a trusted colleague from AAWSAP met with and negotiated with senior executives at Lockheed Martin and hammered out a deal wherein Bigelow’s company, BAASS, would receive a quantity of unusual material that had been stashed away and protected at a facility in California. That material was not made here.”

 Note that Knapp did not claim a full saucer, only “unusual material.”

 Now, in 2026, Jay Stratton has expanded the claim yet again, writing in Out of the Shadows that Ryder had informed him about a vast, decades-long conspiracy, that every UFO crash story was true, that Lockheed had a dozen UFOs in a hangar, and that he would facilitate the transfer of one to Stratton at AAWSAP. 

Ryder described how the hardware—crafts of non-human origin—in their possession came from a variety of incidents, some as high-profile as Roswell. Because he opened that door, I asked what he knew about Roswell. He said that there was indeed a crash in Roswell, New Mexico, in 1947. The craft broke into two pieces, and everything was recovered—the craft and non-human bodies—and sent to the Foreign Technology Division at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio. Everything he shared matched what both Hal and Eric had told me previously, down to the smallest detail.

 According to him, Lockheed had twelve recovered craft of non-human origin in total at that time. Some came with biological occupants. Some were dead on arrival. Others, allegedly, were alive but later perished, refusing food or contact. Communication was limited and often futile. Some of what had been discovered, Ryder told me, was so disturbing that it led individuals involved to resign, suffer mental breakdowns, and in some cases, take their own lives. The truth was just too difficult for them to process.

 He made it clear Lockheed was not the only defense contractor in possession of recovered craft of non-human origin.

​Stratton also claimed that Eric Davis “confirmed” all of the details, despite having denied them earlier.

 Note that Stratton’s version of the claim is incompatible with McMillan’s version, as the craft can’t both have been with Lockheed since 1947 and also transferred to them in 1977. Stratton’s claims aren’t even compatible with themselves. He has Ryder say that Lockheed had twelve flying saucers, some with dead aliens, but also had him say—on the same page!—that Lockheed was only given a “sliver” of the big picture, involving only bits of a propulsion system: “Lockheed was given exotic materials to work on reverse engineering under strict government control, through government-furnished equipment clauses and subcontracts routed through the U.S. Air Force.” It’s possible that he meant that the CIA kept control over the UFOs in Lockheed’s basement and wouldn’t let them touch them, but that rather beggars belief if Ryder’s other alleged claim—that other contractors were working on different parts of the same question—is to be believed, unless you think in plausible that hundreds of aliens spaceships rain down from the sky so everyone can have one without anyone else ever seeing them. It is like the U.S. government had an ET Oprah: “You get a UFO, and you get a UFO!”

 There are many such discrepancies across the versions, as there are with any myth, strongly suggesting that this is an oral story that circulated and mutated across government UFO investigators before surfacing in public after 2019.

 I don’t think there is enough evidence—and certainly nothing independent of the Bigelow/Puthoff circle of ufologists—to draw firm conclusions. But it would be reasonable to suspect that material collected in the 1950s and 1960s during the Project Bluebook era remained in the collection of defense contractors who were asked to study it at the time. We know from declassified documents that the government collected alleged UFO debris that was in reality industrial waste, interesting rocks, amateur electronics, and downed Soviet technology. It would not surprise me if there is more of the same type of material that was never declassified, some of which the CIA may have still considered secret in the 2000s. That would allow most of the characters involved to be telling some version of the truth, though with ever-growing exaggeration and detail due to the telephone-style chain of transmission and the bias of Disclosure advocates, who mistake personal connections and friendships for evidence and accuracy.
